BODex: Scalable Dexterous Grasp Synthesi.narr: Grasping a complex object like a mug or tool with a dexterous hand (16+ joints) involves searching over an enormous space of possible contact points and configurations. BODex solves force closure via bilevel optimization: the inner loop (quadratic program) enforces that contact forces can resist a push from any direction, while the outer loop scales dataset generation by finding high-quality solutions. The payoff is a tractable pipeline that generates thousands of valid grasps from geometry alone, with no real-world data needed.
BODex: Scalable Dexterous Grasp Synthesi.how:
The problem: Given a 3D mesh and a hand with N fingers, find contact points (position + orientation per finger) such that the grasp matrix G (the wrench-generating rows from each contact's geometry) has a positive span — i.e., the grasp achieves force closure. This is a nonlinear search over a huge space.

The mechanism: BODex uses bilevel optimization: (1) Inner loop: a QP that, given hand pose, finds contact points enforcing force-closure constraints (‖Gf‖² minimized, positive weights f ≥ 0). (2) Outer loop: evolutionary search or gradient-based methods that adjust hand configuration (palm pose, finger angles) to maximize the quality metric returned by the inner loop. (3) Physics refinement: run contact simulation (collision-free, stable) on the top K candidates.

Why it works: Decoupling the search (outer loop, discrete) from the verification (inner loop, smooth QP) makes the problem tractable. Repeating this across random configurations and objects builds a large diverse dataset of valid grasps.

GeoDexGrasp: Geometry-aware, Physics-pla.narr: A grasp synthesis system that ignores the object's actual shape class (mug vs. wrench) may compute grasps that work in theory but fail in simulation or reality due to penetration, misalignment, or wrong contact normals. GeoDexGrasp adds geometry awareness: an equivariant encoder splits the object into pose (position/orientation) and shape parts, then physics-aware refinement removes invalid grasps. The lever is equivariance — respecting geometric symmetries reduces sample complexity and improves generalization across object classes.
GeoDexGrasp: Geometry-aware, Physics-pla.how:
The problem: Grasp synthesis generates candidates geometrically, but many fail when contact physics is checked (deep penetration, friction too low, hand self-collision). Physics refinement is expensive (one simulation per candidate, minutes for a dataset).

The mechanism: (1) Equivariant representation: encoder maps object point clouds to a pose descriptor (SE(3) on the object) + shape latent (invariant under object rotation). (2) Grasp generator conditions on the shape latent, not the raw pose, so it learns shape-conditional strategies (e.g., 'cups grasp the rim'). (3) Physics refinement: differentiable simulator evaluates grasps, runs in parallel, filtering the worst 60% before expensive collision checks. (4) Penetration metric: per-contact depth relative to surface normal, optimized away via gradient descent.

Why it works: Splitting pose and shape removes spurious correlations (e.g., learning object orientation rather than grasping strategy). Physics early (before sim) cuts 40% penetration errors and rejects infeasible grasps before expensive simulation.

MaskDexGrasp: Generative Masked Modeling.narr: A mug's handle is a better grasp point than the body; a tool's shaft than its head. But classical grasp synthesis has no notion of semantic parts — it treats the object as an undifferentiated surface. MaskDexGrasp adds part semantics: a masked transformer learns an anatomical part codebook (handle, bowl, spout for a mug), then conditionally generates grasps per part. Part awareness makes grasps both task-aware and editable — the user can request 'grasp the handle' and the model adapts the finger placement.
MaskDexGrasp: Generative Masked Modeling.how:
The problem: Generic grasp synthesis ignores semantic parts. Even a high-quality force-closure grasp on the bowl of a mug may be wrong if the task demands handing it to someone (which requires grasping the handle safely).

The mechanism: (1) Part codebook learning: VQ-VAE learns a discrete codebook of anatomical part embeddings (handle, spout, body, etc.) on a dataset of part-annotated 3D objects. (2) Masked modeling: transformer predicts masked-out part tokens from visible parts (autoregressive or masked-language-model style). (3) Conditional grasp generation: once parts are identified (or user-specified), a separate transformer samples grasp configurations conditioned on the part embedding. (4) Per-finger editing: user can specify 'thumb on handle, fingers on bowl' and the model adjusts the grasp to satisfy constraints.

Why it works: Part semantics reduce the search space (grasping the handle is a smaller, more coherent set than any contact on the mug) and make the system interpretable and user-controllable, unlike black-box neural graspers.

Qdgset: a Large-Scale Grasping Dataset v.narr: Creating a large dataset of valid grasps by simulation is expensive: most randomly sampled grasps fail force-closure tests. Quality-diversity search flips the problem: instead of 'find the best grasp,' it asks 'find many grasps, each good in a different way.' Quality-diversity optimization fills a diversity map with high-quality solutions, ensuring the dataset spans many grasp styles (antipodal, power, pinch) and object poses. This single algorithmic shift turns a thin set of 'optimized' grasps into a rich distribution that learned models can fit.
Qdgset: a Large-Scale Grasping Dataset v.how:
The problem: Grasp datasets trained on a narrow set of high-quality 'winners' teach a policy to overfit to a single style. Real objects afford many valid grasps, and a learned policy should capture that diversity. Growing such a dataset by random sampling and filtering is extremely slow.

The mechanism: Quality-diversity algorithms (e.g., MAP-Elites) maintain a grid (diversity map) where each cell is defined by a behavior descriptor (e.g., contact location on the object, hand orientation). The algorithm iteratively: (1) Samples a grasp config; (2) Simulates it, measuring both quality (success rate, wrench resistance) and the behavior descriptor; (3) If the quality is better than the incumbent in that cell, replace it. (4) The result is a population of grasps spanning the behavior space, each locally optimized.

Why it works: MAP-Elites incentivizes both quality and diversity without explicit multi-objective scalarization. A learned grasp detector trained on Qdgset learns a mode-seeking policy naturally because the data itself is multimodal and the model's diversity helps it generalize.

DextER: Language-driven Dexterous Grasp.narr: Most grasp systems operate in a vacuum: 'where should the fingers go?' But real grasping is task-laden: you grasp a knife by the blade to hand it over, by the handle to cut. DextER embeds language-driven task reasoning into grasp generation. An autoregressive token model (discrete contact tokens) reasons over object affordances and language instructions, then generates contact sequences explicitly. Contact-token autoregression makes reasoning transparent — you can see which finger touches where and why, unlike a black-box neural network.
DextER: Language-driven Dexterous Grasp.how:
The problem: Language-conditional grasping requires bridging two gaps: (1) from language ('hand the knife') to task semantics ('grasp the blade'); (2) from semantics to contact points. End-to-end networks struggle with interpretability and often hallucinate contacts unrelated to the language.

The mechanism: (1) Embodied reasoning module: VLM (or fine-tuned transformer) reasons step-by-step over the scene, object, and language ('To hand a knife, I should grasp the blade away from the sharp edge'). (2) Contact token vocabulary: discrete codebook of contact primitives (e.g., 'thumb on handle, index at edge, pressure 2 N'). (3) Autoregressive generation: language embedding + scene embedding condition a transformer that generates contact tokens one by one (thumb, then index, etc.), each outputting a discrete contact pose. (4) Physics validation: each predicted contact is checked for force closure with already-placed contacts.

Why it works: Discrete contact tokens bottleneck the model to physically valid sequences (must close the grasp) and make the decision tree interpretable. The autoregressive formulation naturally handles the sequential nature of finger placement (some contacts must come before others to avoid self-collision).

GraspSAM: When Segment Anything Meets Gr.narr: Segment Anything Model (SAM) is a foundation model trained on billions of pixels to segment anything on cue. GraspSAM asks: can we adapt SAM to segment and detect grasps? The answer is yes, with light adapters. A user points to an object ('prompt this object for grasps') and a small adapter layer fine-tunes SAM's mask to the grasp domain. Prompting replaces training — the same foundation model adapts to new objects, scenes, and even gripper types without retraining.
GraspSAM: When Segment Anything Meets Gr.how:
The problem: Grasp detection requires both segmentation (which pixels are the object) and pose estimation (where/how to grasp). Training a detector from scratch on new objects is slow. SAM can segment, but it knows nothing about grasps.

The mechanism: (1) Foundation model: SAM encoder extracts rich image features (millions of parameters, frozen). (2) Grasp adapter: a small trainable head (few hundred parameters) learns to map SAM's features to grasp-relevant masks and confidence scores. (3) Prompt types: point (click on object), box, or mask prompt tells SAM which object to focus on. (4) Multi-scale decoding: adapter operates at multiple scales (coarse to fine) to handle small grippers and large objects. (5) Grasp pose regression: from the segmented region, regress 6-DoF gripper pose (center, orientation, width).

Why it works: SAM's pre-training on diverse segmentation tasks teaches it rich representations of boundaries and shape, which transfer to grasp boundaries (where the gripper closes). The adapter is tiny, so few-shot fine-tuning (even zero-shot prompting) works. Different gripper types require only prompt variation, not retraining.

NeuGrasp: Material-Agnostic Grasp Detect.narr: Transparent glass, reflective metal, and translucent plastic are invisible to standard depth sensors: the depth image is garbage or missing. A robot that depends on depth for grasp detection fails on these materials. NeuGrasp learns to reconstruct the hidden surface: a neural SDF (signed-distance function) trained on multi-view observations infers the likely 3D surface of the transparent object, then grasp detection proceeds on the reconstructed geometry. Neural surface inpainting fills in what the sensor cannot see — a generative model completes the object's shape.
NeuGrasp: Material-Agnostic Grasp Detect.how:
The problem: Transparent, specular, and semi-transparent materials break depth sensors. RGB images alone offer limited surface cues. A robot cannot grasp if it cannot see (or infer) where the object is.

The mechanism: (1) Multi-view collection: move the camera around the object or object around the camera (or both); collect RGB images from 4-6 views. (2) SDF learning: a small MLP(x, y, z) → distance-to-surface is trained to minimize the photo-consistency loss across views (pixels should be sharp when rendered from the SDF at the known poses). (3) Implicit regularization: the SDF naturally prefers smooth surfaces and fills gaps (inpainting) where views disagree. (4) Grasp candidate generation: sample points on the learned SDF surface, compute normals, and generate antipodal grasp pairs. (5) Scoring: grasp quality metrics (contact area, force closure) are evaluated on the reconstructed surface, not the broken depth image.

Why it works: Neural SDFs are continuous and differentiable, so they smoothly interpolate across occlusions and handle specular reflections better than depth fusion. The implicit regularization biases the solution toward plausible (closed, smooth) surfaces even when depth is unreliable.

A Cross-view Fusion Framework for Robust.narr: A single RGB-D view may occlude part of the object or show it at a poor viewing angle for grasp detection. Moving the camera or looking from multiple angles gives much more information: the object's full 3D shape, all grasping surfaces, and confidence in each grasp's feasibility. This paper fuses multi-view RGB-D observations with adaptive attention, where the model learns to weight which views are most informative. Adaptive cross-view attention prioritizes the most confident views — a occlusion-reliable mechanism built into the architecture.
A Cross-view Fusion Framework for Robust.how:
The problem: Single-view grasp detection is brittle: occlusions hide grasping surfaces, viewing angle distortion makes pose estimation noisy, and confidence is hard to calibrate. Multiple views provide redundancy, but naive averaging can muddle occlusions (averaging a grasp on empty air with one on the object).

The mechanism: (1) Multi-view encoder: for each of K views, an image encoder (CNN or ViT) extracts per-pixel features. (2) View alignment: features are warped to a canonical 3D coordinate frame using camera poses (calibrated or estimated via structure-from-motion). (3) Cross-view attention: a transformer layer computes attention weights *across* views, with queries from one view and keys/values from all views. High attention means 'this view is informative here.' (4) Grasp refinement: the fused feature map goes to a pose regressor (6D predictor: x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw) and a quality confidence map. (5) Per-view quality: the attention weights also serve as view-specific confidence scores; if one view is blurry, it gets down-weighted automatically.

Why it works: Learned adaptive attention is more reliable than hardcoded fusion (e.g., averaging) because it can handle occlusions, noise, and blur gracefully. The transformer learns to say 'ignore this blurry view' and 'trust this sharp one,' which single-view or early-fusion methods cannot do.

vMF-Contact: Uncertainty-Aware Evidentia.narr: A grasp detector trained on clean, well-lit data may confidently predict grasps in a cluttered, shadowy bin — and fail. The model does not know what it does not know. vMF-Contact trains the detector to output not just a grasp pose but also uncertainty: aleatoric uncertainty (sensor noise, inherent ambiguity) and epistemic uncertainty (the model's ignorance of out-of-distribution clutter). Evidential learning models belief distributions over poses — von Mises-Fisher (vMF) distributions capture orientation uncertainty, Gaussian distributions capture position uncertainty.
vMF-Contact: Uncertainty-Aware Evidentia.how:
The problem: Neural grasp detectors output point estimates (single pose) without uncertainty. In a cluttered bin, when the scene is ambiguous, the detector should either abstain or flag high uncertainty, but it does not. This leads to 'confident errors' that cause picks to fail.

The mechanism: (1) Evidential system: instead of regressing a single grasp pose, the network outputs parameters of a belief distribution. For orientation: a von Mises-Fisher distribution (concentration κ and mean direction μ on SO(3)). For position: a Gaussian (mean, variance). (2) Loss function: evidential loss encourages the network to widen the variance when uncertain (large κ⁻¹) and narrow it when confident. Incorrect predictions are penalized by both the likelihood and the evidence (how concentrated the distribution is). (3) Aleatoric term: comes from sensor noise; captured by the width of the distribution. (4) Epistemic term: model uncertainty; captured by network dropout or ensemble disagreement, reflected in variance scaling. (5) Inference: sample poses from the belief distribution; if variance is high, the grasp is risky.

Why it works: Evidential learning forces the model to admit doubt when data is ambiguous or out-of-distribution. Clutter introduces high epistemic uncertainty (the model sees occlusions it was not trained on), which inflates the predicted variance, allowing a downstream planner to reject risky grasps or trigger multi-view collection.

ComPose: Unified Completion-Pose for Cat.narr: A partially hidden object (say, a cup inside a bin with another cup on top of it) has an invisible base, but its category (cup) and visible parts (rim, handle) hint at what the full shape should be. ComPose jointly solves shape completion and 6-DoF pose under occlusion: a single model outputs both a completed point cloud and the object's 3D pose. Joint optimization couples geometry and pose — the reconstructed shape is consistent with the observed partial shape and the inferred pose.
ComPose: Unified Completion-Pose for Cat.how:
The problem: Separate completion and pose estimation is suboptimal. A shape-completion model may hallucinate an implausible geometry (e.g., fill the underside with random points), and a pose regressor sees only the partial object, leading to drift. Coupling them constrains the solution space: the completed shape must explain the observations and be pose-consistent.

The mechanism: (1) Category-level prior: during training, the model learns a per-category implicit function (e.g., all mugs share a canonical shape). (2) Partial observation encoding: the visible points (and their mask) are encoded via a point-net encoder. (3) Unified decoder: outputs two heads: (a) shape parameters (deformation of the canonical shape); (b) 6-DoF pose (rotation + translation). (4) Consistency loss: the predicted pose and shape are checked: render the completed shape at the predicted pose; it should match the observed partial points (photo-consistency). (5) Geometric loss: completed shape should be closed, have plausible curvature, not interpenetrate known obstacles.

Why it works: Multi-task learning with a shared representation (encoding + decoder) encourages the model to find a pose and shape that are mutually consistent. A shape completion alone might invent geometry; pose alone might misalign. Together, they reinforce each other.

ViViDex: Vision-Based Dexterous Manipula.narr: A multi-fingered hand can reorient an object in-hand by a sequence of finger lifts and replants (finger gaiting), but this requires precise coordination across 20+ joints. Instead of hand-engineering the policy or learning from sparse real-robot data, ViViDex learns from unlabeled human videos: extract human hand trajectories, compute object motion, then train a vision-based policy with trajectory-guided rewards that encourage the robot to imitate the object motion. Trajectory-guided rewards provide dense learning signal from passive video — no touch sensor, no real-robot interaction needed for training.
ViViDex: Vision-Based Dexterous Manipula.how:
The problem: Learning dexterous manipulation on a real hand is sample-hungry (thousands of trials) and risky (fingers wear out, objects break). Supervised learning from kinesthetic demonstrations is slow. Reward-only RL requires a hand-crafted reward function, which is brittle.

The mechanism: (1) Video dataset: collect human hand videos manipulating objects (e.g., rotating a ball in-hand). (2) Trajectory extraction: use hand-pose and object-pose estimators (HaMeR + FoundationPose) to extract frame-by-frame hand configuration and object position/orientation. (3) Reward function: the robot's reward is the similarity between (a) the observed object trajectory in the video and (b) the object trajectory from the robot's action. Metric: e.g., L2 distance in SO(3) × ℝ³ for object pose, or relative object motion. (4) Vision-only rollout: the policy takes RGB observations from the robot's wrist camera (same camera as the video source). (5) Imitation: RL (e.g., PPO) trains the policy to match the object trajectory, not the hand trajectory (hand geometry differs). (6) Refinement: domain randomize camera pose, lighting, object texture to improve sim-to-real transfer.

Why it works: Using object motion as the reward decouples the learning from the human hand morphology (which differs from the robot's). A video dataset is much cheaper to collect than real-robot data. The vision-only setup (RGB input) transfers to the robot without sensor gaps.

AnyRotate: Gravity-Invariant In-Hand Rot.narr: A policy trained in simulation for in-hand rotation often fails on the real hand because tactile sensing and friction are poorly modeled. AnyRotate addresses this by learning a dense tactile simulation (256 sensors per finger, simulating normal and shear forces) in simulation, then transferring to the real hand with domain randomization and tactile noise injection. The policy is 'gravity-invariant': it does not overfit to gravitational assist (e.g., learning to rotate only along one axis where gravity helps), so it generalizes to rotations in any direction. Dense tactile feedback replaces proprioception — the hand feels when fingers slip and adjusts preemptively.
AnyRotate: Gravity-Invariant In-Hand Rot.how:
The problem: In-hand rotation requires coordinating fingers through contact-mode switches (finger lifts, replants, sliding). Proprioception alone (joint angles) is noisy and does not capture slip. Real hands have friction, finger compliance, and complex contact dynamics that simple models miss. Policies trained on naive force estimates (e.g., normal force from pressure sensors) fail because they do not match reality.

The mechanism: (1) Tactile simulation: Isaac Gym or MuJoCo with a tactile plugin (e.g., Gazebo's GelSight simulation or fabric simulator) computes 256-point sensor array per finger, measuring (Fx, Fy, Fz) and shear stress at each point. (2) Reward: angular error to target orientation + penalty for dropping or slipping (sensor spike beyond threshold). (3) Domain randomization: friction μ ∈ [0.6, 1.2], object mass ±10%, finger stiffness variation, sensor noise ±8 mN. (4) Tactile noise injection: during training, add zero-mean Gaussian to sensor readings, so the learned policy is reliable to sensor noise. (5) Gravity-invariant training: include rotations around all three axes (grasp-frame coordinates) in the training set, not just easy ones. (6) Sim-to-real: transfer the policy directly to a real hand with (optionally) a small number of real-world fine-tuning episodes.

Why it works: Dense tactile feedback gives the policy a direct perception of slip and contact state, making the control loop reactive and reliable. Domain randomization of friction (the hardest-to-model parameter) is key; varied training friction teaches the policy to adapt, reducing sensitivity to friction mismatch between sim and real.

From Simple to Complex Skills: In-Hand O.narr: Learning a single monolithic policy to rotate an object 180° in-hand from random initial poses is hard: the state space is huge and the contact modes jump discontinuously. Instead, this paper decomposes the task into simpler skills: 'rotate-30°', 'regrasp', 'stabilize'. A hierarchical policy learns each skill independently in simulation, then chains them: apply 'rotate-30°' six times to achieve 180°. Skill composition is more stable than end-to-end learning — each skill has a smaller, more consistent problem, so the learned policy is more reliable.
From Simple to Complex Skills: In-Hand O.how:
The problem: A monolithic policy for continuous rotation must handle mode switches (finger lifts and replants) implicitly. When the policy fails, it is unclear if the issue is the continuous angle tracking or the discrete finger coordination. The policy overfits to one grasp type (e.g., rotating fast) and fails on others (e.g., heavy objects that require slower, more careful gait).

The mechanism: (1) Skill definition: design low-level rotation skills (e.g., 'rotate-30°-clockwise', 'regrasp-axis-aligned', 'stabilize'). Each skill has a clear success condition (object angle ±5°, no slip). (2) Skill learning: train each skill independently with RL (PPO, SAC) in simulation. Reward per skill is sparse (success/fail) or shaped (angle error). (3) Hierarchical policy: high-level policy (or hardcoded routine) sequences skills. For 180° rotation: call rotate-30° six times. (4) Tracking: each skill is a closed-loop controller; if skill execution is interrupted (e.g., object slips and angle drifts), regrasp and re-attempt. (5) Fault tolerance: if a skill fails twice, the hierarchical controller triggers a recovery routine (return to a stable intermediate pose).

Why it works: Decomposition reduces complexity per skill and makes each skill's failure mode interpretable. A failed rotate-30° suggests contact is lost; a failed regrasp suggests hand configuration is infeasible. The hierarchical layer is reliable because it is rule-based or learned on a small discrete action space (which skill to run next). This trades off end-to-end learning for interpretability and sample efficiency.

Structural Action Transformer for 3D Dex.narr: A policy learned on one robotic hand (e.g., Shadow Hand with 24 DoF) may not transfer to another hand (e.g., a 16-DoF gripper) because the action spaces are different. Structural Action Transformer sidesteps this by learning a latent space of 'structural' actions: joint motions that are embodiment-agnostic. An embodied joint codebook encodes hand-specific DoF, while flow matching (a generative model) learns the structure of valid action sequences. Embodied codebooks and flow matching enable cross-embodiment transfer — the same learned policy runs on different hands with minor re-indexing.
Structural Action Transformer for 3D Dex.how:
The problem: Each robotic hand has a different number of joints (16 to 24+) and kinematic structure. A policy trained on one hand's action space (16-D or 24-D) does not directly apply to another. Naïve transfer (e.g., interpolate or drop dimensions) loses structure and fails.

The mechanism: (1) Embodied action codebook: each hand type has a VQ-VAE that learns a discrete vocabulary of 'joint groups' (e.g., 'all fingers spread', 'thumb opposes four fingers'). The codebook is trained on demonstrations for that hand and captures recurring muscle-synergy-like motions. (2) Latent action space: instead of outputting raw joint angles, the policy outputs a sequence of codebook indices (discrete tokens). (3) Decoder: for each hand type, a separate decoder maps codebook tokens → hand-specific joint angles. (4) Flow matching: a generative model (flow model, an alternative to diffusion) learns the distribution of valid action sequences (token sequences). The flow model is trained on a multimodal dataset of multiple hand types, learning to generate coherent, physically plausible token sequences. (5) Inference: given a scene observation (object, hand), the flow model samples a token sequence, the hand-specific decoder converts to joint angles, and the hand executes.

Why it works: Embodied codebooks capture hand-specific motor primitives, while flow matching learns the structure of manipulation (sequence, timing, contact modes) that is independent of embodiment. Different hands decode the same tokens differently, enabling cross-embodiment transfer.

Composing Dexterous Grasping and In-Hand.narr: Grasping an object is one task; in-hand rotation is another. Can a single system do both without retraining? Yes, if you reuse the learned components. A critic network (trained via RL for manipulation) scores how suitable a grasp is for the downstream task (e.g., 'this grasp will be stable during a 180° rotation'). When the grasping policy picks among candidate grasps, it uses the critic to rank them. The critic bridges the two tasks — it translates 'will this grasp enable rotation?' into a signal the grasp picker can use.
Composing Dexterous Grasping and In-Hand.how:
The problem: Grasp detection and in-hand manipulation are trained separately. A detected grasp is locally good (force closure), but it may be poor for the next task (e.g., a pencil held at the tip is stable but hard to rotate). The robot re-grasps mid-task, wasting time.

The mechanism: (1) Grasp policy: a network that detects grasps (6-DoF pose, quality) from RGB-D. Trained on grasping success data. (2) Manipulation policy: a dexterous-hand policy trained with RL to rotate objects in-hand, given a grasp pose. During training, the policy sees (state, grasp pose) and learns to execute the rotation. A critic network Q(state, grasp) estimates success probability of rotation starting from that grasp. (3) Reuse: once the manipulation policy and critic are trained, the grasp detection policy is fine-tuned or re-ranked: instead of picking the highest-quality grasp, pick the one with the highest critic score Q(current_state, candidate_grasp). (4) Inference: detect candidate grasps, score each via the critic, pick the best for the downstream task.

Why it works: The critic encapsulates the downstream task's preferences without requiring a new end-to-end grasp dataset. Transfer from one task (manipulation) to another (grasping) is fast because the critic is already learned and the grasp detector just learns a new ranking.

BiFold: Bimanual Cloth Folding with Lang.narr: Folding a shirt requires two hands: one anchors a corner while the other pulls the opposite corner. Each arm's force acts on the shared cloth, and if the arms move at different speeds, the cloth tears or bunches. BiFold uses a VLM to reason about the task from language ('fold the shirt in half toward you'), then a diffusion policy generates joint 12-D future state (positions of both end-effectors) conditioned on the VLM's reasoning. The two arms move simultaneously, and their coordination emerges from the joint state diffusion. Diffusing joint state ensures both arms move coherently — they are not controlled independently.
BiFold: Bimanual Cloth Folding with Lang.how:
The problem: Two-arm cloth manipulation is sensitive to coordination: independent arm policies can work against each other, causing cloth to tear or jam. Naive concatenation of two single-arm policies often fails. The cloth state is complex (point cloud, cloth deformation history) and high-dimensional.

The mechanism: (1) VLM reasoning: GPT-4V is given the scene (cloth, tables, bins) and language instruction ('fold toward you'). VLM outputs a reasoning trace ('First, grasp the left edge with the left hand. Then, fold toward me') and key fold landmarks. (2) Scene encoding: point cloud of the cloth (4,096 points) + two arm proprioception (joint angles) are encoded via a transformer. (3) State diffusion: a diffusion model learns to denoise 12-D future state: (left_EE x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw) + (right_EE x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw). Conditioning includes the VLM embedding and the current scene encoding. (4) Denoising loop: 50 DDPM steps at 20 Hz produce a smooth trajectory. (5) Inverse dynamics: the predicted joint state is converted to arm joint angles and velocities via inverse kinematics (analytical for 6-DoF arms, or a learned IK network). (6) Execution: both arms receive joint commands simultaneously; the cloth moves coherently because the diffusion model learned to couple the two arms during training.

Why it works: Diffusing joint state of both arms ensures they are modeled jointly, not independently. The VLM provides high-level semantics ('fold away' vs. 'fold toward'), which the diffusion model translates to coordinated motion. The point-cloud representation is invariant to cloth deformation, so the model learns the task structure, not memorized cloth shapes.

Learning Coordinated Bimanual Policies w.narr: This paper proposes a general system for learning bimanual policies: diffuse the future scene state (both arms and objects), conditioned on observations, then decode the state to actions via inverse dynamics. Unlike task-specific methods, this approach is agnostic to the task (fold, carry, catch) and the state representation (point cloud, voxel, keypoint). State diffusion as a general bimanual interface decouples high-level reasoning from low-level control — a planner predicts 'where both arms should be,' and inverse dynamics makes it happen.
Learning Coordinated Bimanual Policies w.how:
The problem: Writing separate bimanual policies for folding, carrying, catching, etc., is tedious. A general system that works across tasks would amortize the learning cost. Single-arm policies fail on tasks requiring coordination because they optimize independently.

The mechanism: (1) State representation: choose a common representation for scene state (e.g., point cloud of cloth + EE positions, or keypoints of objects + arm poses). (2) State diffusion model: a diffusion model (DDPM) learns to generate plausible future states conditioned on past observations and language (if available). The model operates on the latent space of the state representation. (3) Inference: given current observation, run denoising loop to sample a future state; the model learns to output coordinated arm positions. (4) Inverse dynamics: a separate IK solver (analytical, learned, or semi-analytical) converts the predicted joint state to joint torques/actions. Apply to both arms. (5) Residual learning: optionally, add a small residual policy on top of the inverse-dynamics solution to adapt to real-world friction and dynamics.

Why it works: Decoupling state-prediction from action-decoding makes the system modular: the diffusion model is task-agnostic (it learns to predict plausible states), while the inverse-dynamics layer is arm-agnostic. The same diffusion model can power many tasks; new tasks require only new training data, not new policy architecture.

Active Vision for Bimanual Robotic Manip.narr: When one arm manipulates an object and the second arm helps, the first arm often occludes the object from the robot's fixed wrist camera. Active Vision solves this by dedicating the second arm to carrying a camera: while the main arm folds cloth or pours, the 'active' camera arm moves to maintain a clear view of the manipulation site. A separate vision arm decouples perception from actuation — the main arm can move freely without worrying about occlusions.
Active Vision for Bimanual Robotic Manip.how:
The problem: Fixed wrist cameras (mounted on the manipulating arm) occlude the very objects the arm is trying to manipulate. Multi-view fusion from different fixed cameras in the workspace helps, but many small objects are invisible from workspace cameras. A camera on the end-effector can follow the manipulation, but then the end-effector is holding a camera, not a gripper.

The mechanism: (1) Two-arm system: one arm ('actor') manipulates; one arm ('vision') holds a camera. (2) Perception policy: a small network predicts good camera poses (position + orientation) given the current scene observation and the actor arm's state. Camera poses are ranked by estimated view quality (entropy of the observed object region, occlusion-free pixels). (3) Active camera planner: every N steps, the vision arm is commanded to move the camera to a high-quality pose. Path planning is done in real-time (RRT or sampling-based). (4) Scene observation: fused from (a) the active camera and (b) optionally, fixed workspace cameras. (5) Actor policy: conditioned on the fused observations (actor can now see the workspace clearly because the vision arm is positioning the camera). The actor executes the main task.

Why it works: Separating the camera from the gripper removes a DoF conflict: the gripper can move to the object without the camera losing sight of it. The vision arm's movements are optimized for perception (follow the manipulation), not actuation (apply forces), so simple control (e.g., inverse kinematics) suffices.

Learning Dexterous Bimanual Catch Skills.narr: Catching requires both arms to move in concert, reaching to intercept a flying ball and 'closing' the grasp in the right frame. This is a high-speed, contact-rich coordination task that is hard to learn. This paper uses adversarial-cooperative RL: a 'thrower' agent learns to throw the ball in ways that the 'catcher' agents must cooperate to catch. Adversarial training (the thrower tries to make catching hard) pushes the catcher to explore diverse catching strategies and coordinate both arms. Adversarial curriculum makes the task progressively harder, forcing generalization — the catcher learns to adapt, not just memorize a single throw.
Learning Dexterous Bimanual Catch Skills.how:
The problem: Bimanual catching is a coordination task where the two arms must meet at the right place and time, and timing is critical (frame-perfect). A single-arm catcher can catch some trajectories but not others (e.g., those requiring two hands to intercept). Learning the distribution of valid cooperative catch strategies requires a rich training curriculum.

The mechanism: (1) Multi-agent RL: three agents (or one adversarial + two cooperative). Agents share a simulator and reward structure. (2) Thrower agent: learns to generate ball-throw trajectories. Reward: inverse of catcher success (adversarial loss). The thrower explores throwing styles that the catcher cannot handle. (3) Catcher agents (left + right arms): learn to coordinate and catch. Reward: catching success (ball inside closed hands). Communication: if allowed, catchers can exchange observations or emergent signals. (4) Curriculum: as the thrower learns harder throws, the catcher is forced to generalize. Early in training, the thrower throws easy balls; as catchers improve, the thrower throws harder. (5) Symmetry: because catching is symmetric (left/right arms), the learned policy can be transferred or mirrored.

Why it works: Adversarial training provides a natural curriculum: the difficulty level self-adjusts. Cooperative multi-agent RL encourages the two arm policies to specialize and complement each other (e.g., one arm intercepts, the other closes). The result is 2× better performance than single-arm RL on the same catch tasks, and better generalization to new throw types not seen during training.

ForceVLA2: Hybrid Force-Position Control.narr: Inserting a USB plug requires the robot to regulate force (the plug must be pressed with just-right firmness, not too hard or soft) while tracking a position (the plug must stay centered in the port). Pure position control ignores the force, leading to jamming or breakage. ForceVLA2 is a vision-language model (VLA) augmented with force awareness: a mixture-of-experts (MoE) head learns to predict a force-aware residual action that adjusts the position when force feedback signals a problem (e.g., 'force is too high, back off'). Force-aware MoE learns task-specific force strategies — each task (insertion, wiping, pressing) gets its own force policy.
ForceVLA2: Hybrid Force-Position Control.how:
The problem: Standard VLAs (pixel-to-action models) output position or velocity commands, not force commands. Force control requires a separate feedback loop: measure force, compute compliance response, update position. Naive integration (run VLA, then add a force correction layer) can conflict or be too slow.

The mechanism: (1) Vision-language encoder: encodes scene (RGB) and task language ('insert USB plug') into a latent vector. (2) MoE gate: learns to select which expert to use based on the current force feedback and task. (3) Expert policies: each expert is a small network trained for a specific task (insertion, wiping, etc.) and learns to output a position residual (Δx, Δy, Δz) when force feedback indicates a problem. (4) Force signal: 6-axis F/T sensor (wrist-mounted) measures Fx, Fy, Fz, τx, τy, τz at 50–100 Hz. (5) Gating logic: if |Fxy| > threshold (lateral force too high), gate selects the 'centering' expert, which outputs a residual that steers the plug back to center. If Fz > threshold (axial force too high), gate selects 'back-off' expert, which retracts slightly. (6) Closed-loop control: position commands from the VLA + residuals from MoE → joint commands → executed in real-time.

Why it works: MoE decouples different force-control strategies (insertion vs. wiping) without requiring a monolithic model. Force feedback is reactive (50 ms loop) while the VLA runs at 10 Hz, so force control handles high-frequency disturbances. The residual structure preserves the VLA's action while modulating it for force, preventing large corrections that break the grasp.

Adaptive Compliance Policy: Learning Com.narr: A robot pushing a peg into a hole needs to be compliant (soft) so it yields when the peg jams, but the amount of compliance varies: too stiff and the peg breaks; too soft and it takes forever. Classical impedance control uses fixed stiffness parameters, which is brittle. Adaptive Compliance Policy learns spatiotemporal stiffness profiles from demonstrations: a diffusion policy predicts, for each time step, a 6-D compliance vector (how stiff the end-effector should be in each direction). Learned compliance adapts to the task and phase of execution — soft when approaching, stiff when in contact.
Adaptive Compliance Policy: Learning Com.how:
The problem: Contact-rich tasks (insertion, assembly, surface wiping) require dynamic compliance: the stiffness should change as the task progresses (approach → soft, contact → medium, push → stiff) and adapt to the environment (hard surface → stiffer; deformable surface → softer). Fixed impedance parameters cannot capture this, and tuning per-task is expensive.

The mechanism: (1) Demonstration collection: humans teleoperate the robot to solve the task (insertion, wiping, etc.). Record RGB observations, joint angles, joint torques, and optionally force-feedback if available. (2) Compliance extraction: for each demo, compute the 'compliance' implicit in the actions: high acceleration → low inferred stiffness; low acceleration + high force → high inferred stiffness. Or, if force is available, directly measure compliance (Kz = Fz / δz for motion in z). (3) Diffusion model: a diffusion policy learns to denoise action chunks, where each action includes both (position/velocity command, compliance vector). Conditioning: RGB observation + proprioceptive state + task label. (4) Spatial compliance: Kx, Ky, Kz, τx, τy, τz are learned separately; the model learns when to make x-direction stiff (during approach) vs. soft (when in contact). (5) Inference: diffusion model samples both position and compliance; the robot's control loop applies the sampled compliance (e.g., impedance controller with Kz = sampled_Kz).

Why it works: Learning compliance from demonstrations captures the task structure (when to be soft/stiff) implicitly. Diffusion models are good at modeling multimodal distributions (many valid compliance profiles for a task), so the learned policy is more reliable than a single fixed compliance. Spatiotemporal learning allows compliance to change over the trajectory, adapting to transient events (jamming, slipping) without explicit mode detection.

Tactile-Driven Non-Prehensile Manipulati.narr: Pushing an object on a table, the robot can control whether the object sticks (high friction, moves with the pusher) or slides (low friction, glides under the pusher). The transition from stick to slide is called the contact mode. Without tactile sensing, a robot cannot know which mode it is in, so it cannot plan reliable pushes. Tactile-Driven Non-Prehensile Manipulation uses tactile feedback (optical or capacitive pressure sensors on the pusher) to detect contact mode and adjust the push strategy. Tactile sensing lets the robot feel and switch between stick and slide on demand — a feedback mechanism that enables reliable pushing without a physics model.
Tactile-Driven Non-Prehensile Manipulati.how:
The problem: Pushing requires reasoning about friction and contact modes, which are difficult to model accurately. Friction varies with surface texture, humidity, and contact area. A push command 'move 5 cm forward' might slide 3 cm or stick and move 5 cm, depending on unmodeled friction. Without feedback, the robot cannot adapt.

The mechanism: (1) Tactile sensor: an array of pressure sensors on the pusher (e.g., GelSight or capacitive strips) measures normal force and shear stress at the contact surface. (2) Contact mode detection: compute the ratio of shear to normal force. If Fshear / Fnormal < μ (friction coefficient), the contact is sticking (high friction resistance). If Fshear / Fnormal ≈ 1, the contact is sliding (kinetic friction). (3) Extrinsic mode control: the robot does not model the object; instead, it observes the tactile signal and reacts. For example: 'if shear stress is low, push harder (apply more normal force to increase stick)' or 'if shear is high, reduce normal force to slide.' (4) Gradient optimization: formulate the desired contact mode as a loss function (e.g., target shear ~0.8 × Fnormal). Use tactile observations to compute gradients and adjust pusher orientation/normal force online. (5) Learning: can also train a neural network to map (tactile signal, object state) → (next pusher action), learning the stick/slide switching policy from interaction data.

Why it works: Tactile feedback closes the control loop at high frequency (~100 Hz), allowing the robot to react to unexpected friction or slipping within milliseconds. Gradient-based online optimization makes the approach model-free: the robot does not need a friction coefficient or object model, only the ability to sense and react. This simplicity makes it reliable to unmodeled phenomena (moisture, contamination).

Contact-Aware Neural Dynamics.narr: Learning a forward dynamics model (predicting the next state from the current state and action) is hard in contact-rich tasks because the physics jumps discontinuously when contact is made or broken. Standard neural networks average across modes, leading to mushy predictions. Contact-Aware Neural Dynamics augments learning with tactile co-training: a second head predicts contact state (in contact or not) from the same observations, and the dynamics model is trained jointly. Tactile co-training implicitly aligns the learned dynamics with real contact transitions — the model learns to predict contact before the dynamics jumps.
Contact-Aware Neural Dynamics.how:
The problem: Forward models trained on contact-rich data (e.g., pushing, grasping) tend to average over the discontinuities in dynamics. When contact happens, the equations of motion change, but the neural network sees both 'before contact' and 'after contact' examples and learns an averaged model that is accurate in neither regime.

The mechanism: (1) Dual-head architecture: one head predicts next state (δx, Δθ), another predicts contact (binary or multiclass: 'free', 'in-contact', 'sliding'). (2) Data collection: collect trajectories with ground-truth contact labels (e.g., from touch sensors or force thresholds). (3) Joint training: loss = L_dynamics (predicted state vs. observed) + λ L_contact (predicted contact vs. observed). (4) Implicit alignment: by predicting contact, the model learns to separate the data into contact regimes. The dynamics head then specializes: free-flight dynamics are learned from 'free' examples, contact dynamics from 'in-contact' examples. (5) Inference: when predicting the next state, the model first predicts contact; depending on the prediction, it applies the appropriate dynamics (via implicit routing or explicit mode-switching). (6) Real-world co-training: optionally, collect real data with real touch sensors and train the model to predict real tactile signals, not just simulation contact labels. This closes the sim-to-real gap.

Why it works: Tactile co-training forces the model to learn a latent factorization of the dynamics (free vs. contact), improving accuracy on both regimes. The auxiliary contact task acts as an inductive bias: predicting contact is a harder, more informative task than just modeling dynamics, so it guides the shared representation toward physically meaningful features. Real-world tactile co-training further aligns the model with real sensor data, reducing sim-to-real transfer error.

DeformPAM: Data-Efficient Long-Horizon D.narr: Cloth and rope have effectively infinite degrees of freedom — no fixed shape to grasp. When a robot pulls a corner of a shirt, the rest deforms in ways no camera can fully predict from a single view. The core problem: predict how the object will reshape under an action, well enough to plan the next move. DeformPAM learns a dynamics model from multiview point clouds, trained on preference labels rather than hard supervision, letting the robot find its own motion strategy without needing a per-object physics simulator.
DeformPAM: Data-Efficient Long-Horizon D.how:
The problem: Deformable objects have no canonical pose; their state is a high-dimensional point cloud. A gripper action (pick-place) creates a complex deformation that a unimodal predictor would average into a mushy guess.

The mechanism:

  1. Collect 40,000 random pick-place trajectories on real cloth (or in sim); record the point cloud before and after.
  2. Train a diffusion model on the point-cloud deltas, conditioned on the action embedding.
  3. At test time, use preference learning: collect human labels on which rollout outcome is ‘better’ (closer to flat, say), then fine-tune the diffusion model with that signal.
  4. Plan by sampling multiple futures from the diffusion model and picking the best under the learned preference.

Why it works: Preference alignment avoids the need for a per-object simulator and lets the robot learn a task-aligned cost directly from comparison labels, making the model both data-efficient and task-aware.

General-Purpose Clothes Manipulation wit.narr: Folding, flattening, and hanging a shirt are three different tasks, yet they share a common structure: grasp a semantic part (a hem, a sleeve) and move it to a goal location. Rather than learn three separate policies, the key insight is to predict sparse semantic keypoints (sleeve, hem, neckline) that generalize across tasks, then learn a single policy that operates on those keypoints regardless of task or garment size.
General-Purpose Clothes Manipulation wit.how:
The problem: A generic ‘fold’ policy fails when the shirt is a different size or material; re-learning for each variant is impractical.

The mechanism:

  1. Annotate human demonstrations with semantic part labels (sleeve, hem, collar, etc.).
  2. Train a neural network to predict keypoint locations from the point cloud, outputting 2D or 3D coordinates for each semantic part.
  3. Represent the action as ‘move this keypoint to this location’ rather than joint angles.
  4. A low-level controller (inverse kinematics + motion planning) turns keypoint deltas into gripper commands.

Why it works: Semantic keypoints are invariant to size and material variation; the policy learns the task intent, not the geometry, so a single model handles folds, flattens, and hangs.

Learning Object Properties via Different.narr: Cloth deformation depends on material properties — stiffness, density, friction — that are invisible. If a robot blindly applies the same pushing force to silk versus denim, it will fail on one. The robot must use its own actions as a probe: push the fabric and watch how it bends, then invert that observation to infer the material properties. Differentiable simulation lets the robot jointly optimize the action and the hidden material parameters to match the observed outcome.
Learning Object Properties via Different.how:
The problem: Deformable properties are unknown; the robot can only observe the result of its actions, not the material parameters directly.

The mechanism:

  1. Initialize unknown material parameters (elasticity modulus, damping, friction) with a broad prior.
  2. Execute a probe action (a push or poke) on the real cloth; record the resulting deformation via proprioception or visual tracking.
  3. In the differentiable simulator, roll forward the same action using the current material estimates.
  4. Backprop the error between simulated and observed deformation through the differentiable physics engine to update the material parameters.
  5. Repeat with different actions to refine the estimates.

Why it works: Differentiable simulation turns perception into an inverse-physics problem, allowing the robot to learn hidden properties from the gap between prediction and reality without explicit labels.

Shared Control for Cable Routing with Ta.narr: Routing a cable or rope around obstacles is hard: the robot must maintain contact (to guide the cable) without pinching or kinking it, and the cable can slip under its gripper. Simple position control will miss the cable when it slips; pure force control can over-squeeze. Shared control divides authority between high-level motion planning and low-level tactile feedback, letting the robot steer the overall path while the tactile loop adjusts grip pressure and angle moment-to-moment.
Shared Control for Cable Routing with Ta.how:
The problem: Cable routing requires simultaneous path following and force regulation; one high-level controller cannot do both without oscillating.

The mechanism:

  1. High-level planner computes a desired end-effector trajectory around obstacles (using RRT or similar).
  2. At each step, a tactile sensor on the gripper detects slip (shear force spikes) and contact loss (sudden normal-force dip).
  3. If slip is detected, the low-level tactile controller increases grip pressure and adjusts the approach angle to re-align the cable.
  4. If contact is lost, it backs up and re-engages.
  5. Authority sharing: the planner commits to the high-level path, but the tactile loop refines the grasp parameters online.

Why it works: Tactical sensing provides millisecond-scale feedback that position planning cannot; decoupling trajectory from grasp quality lets each work at its natural timescale.

ReloPush: Multi-Object Rearrangement wit.narr: Moving 20 objects in a confined space without grasping — just pushing with a flat arm — is faster than picking but requires predicting where each object will land after a push. The core challenge is planning a push sequence that doesn’t jam one object against an obstacle mid-sequence. ReloPush builds a push-reachability graph: each node is a pose, each edge is a feasible push, and graph search finds a collision-free rearrangement sequence.
ReloPush: Multi-Object Rearrangement wit.how:
The problem: A naive push can slide an object into a dead end; planning has to see ahead multiple steps and avoid traps.

The mechanism:

  1. Discretize the table into cells (4 cm grid); compute the limit-surface friction model for the pusher-object pair (quasi-static mechanics).
  2. For each object, precompute which poses it can reach from its current position via a straight push; mark reachable neighbors in a graph.
  3. Build a global rearrangement graph where each node is a scene configuration (positions of all objects) and edges represent sequences of individual pushes.
  4. Run A* with a learned heuristic (MLP trained on random scenes) to find the shortest rearrangement path.
  5. For each push in the plan, apply MPPI online to correct for model error; sample 512 push trajectories and pick the one that best tracks the reference.

Why it works: Push-graph abstraction decomposes the combinatorial rearrangement problem into reachability (solvable with friction models) and graph search (solvable with A*); online MPPI closes the model gap at execution time.

Dynamic Object-Goal Pushing with Mobile.narr: A mobile manipulator (arm on a wheeled base) can push objects across a room, but it must coordinate the arm and base so neither overshoots the goal. Constrained RL is the tool: learn a push policy that respects position constraints (don’t go past this line) and force constraints (don’t slam into walls) from experience, without manual trajectory specification. The key is to encode the constraints as differentiable costs that the RL algorithm minimizes alongside reward.
Dynamic Object-Goal Pushing with Mobile.how:
The problem: Pushing with a mobile base adds a degree of freedom (base position) that standard manipulation policies don’t handle; naive RL will learn to overshoot because there’s no penalty for hitting the boundary.

The mechanism:

  1. Define a hard constraint: object must stay within a goal region (e.g., a 0.5 m zone); formalize as ‘distance to boundary ≥ 0’.
  2. In each RL step, compute the constraint violation (negative if violated) and add it as a penalty to the reward.
  3. Use a constrained RL algorithm (e.g., Lagrangian dual descent or CPO) that maintains feasibility: the policy adapts its strategy to satisfy constraints while maximizing reward.
  4. Simulate the full manipulator + object dynamics; sample push actions and roll forward 1–2 seconds in simulation.
  5. The learned policy outputs joint velocities for both arm and base, coordinating them reactively.

Why it works: Constrained RL avoids hand-crafted reach-avoidance controllers; the policy learns the coupling between arm and base motion from experience, adapting to different object masses and friction without re-tuning.

Goal-Driven Robotic Pushing Under Uncert.narr: A push’s outcome depends on the object’s mass and the table’s friction — neither of which the robot knows precisely. Applying a preset push trajectory will land the object far from the goal if the mass is wrong. Model-predictive path integral (MPPI) control samples a distribution of push directions and magnitudes, evaluates each in a fast physics model that varies mass and friction, and commits to the direction that best reaches the goal on average.
Goal-Driven Robotic Pushing Under Uncert.how:
The problem: Physics-based push planning requires knowing mass and friction; without them, a single open-loop push fails. Replanning on each push is slow.

The mechanism:

  1. Maintain a distribution over unknown properties: mass ∈ [100g, 500g], friction μ ∈ [0.1, 0.8].
  2. At each step, sample 512 push trajectories (direction θ, magnitude α) from a proposal distribution centered on the nominal best push.
  3. For each sample, roll the object forward using the physics model at 10 random (mass, friction) pairs; score it as the expected distance to goal.
  4. Weight each trajectory by its expected score and re-estimate the proposal distribution (cross-entropy method).
  5. Execute the best trajectory; observe the actual outcome and update the property distribution via Bayes rule.

Why it works: MPPI handles uncertainty by averaging over multiple physics models; sampling avoids the need to differentiate through the friction law (which is non-smooth). Iterative refinement of the property posterior keeps planning adaptive.

Dynamic On-Palm Manipulation via Control.narr: Rather than lift an object, a dexterous hand can slide it across its palm — rotating it, flipping it, or exchanging it between fingers. This ‘non-prehensile’ manipulation is faster than finger gaiting and uses less energy, but requires precise control of where the object is touching. Contact-implicit MPC plans by computing the contact forces that would slide the object to a target pose, rather than planning trajectories explicitly.
Dynamic On-Palm Manipulation via Control.how:
The problem: Sliding is a mode where friction acts tangentially; predicting the slide motion and controlling it requires modeling the contact, which changes as the object moves.

The mechanism:

  1. State is object pose (position + orientation) and contact position (which part of the object is touching which finger).
  2. At each time step, MPC solves: find contact forces and hand motion that minimize distance to the goal, subject to ‘the object slides (does not lift or rotate unexpectedly)’.
  3. Enforce the slide constraint by requiring: the contact normal force ≥ 0 (touching) and the tangential force ≤ μ × normal force (sticking, not slipping).
  4. The solver (Convex-Concave Procedure or similar) iterates: predict how the object moves under the candidate forces, refine the contact model, adjust forces.
  5. Execute the best forces for 100 ms; re-plan at the next step.

Why it works: Contact-implicit methods avoid the need to explicitly model the contact schedule (when it breaks, when it remakes); they encode sliding constraints directly and let the solver find feasible force trajectories. Online replanning corrects for model errors.

Robotic Hand Tool Use with Contact-Based.narr: Grasping a tool is not enough; the robot must feel the tool and control forces through it, not at its own fingers. A peeler that is gripped too hard will bend; one moved too fast will tear the vegetable. The task is learned from human demonstrations, but the key is to copy the contact sequence and force profile, not the trajectory. A quick stiffness-identification step calibrates the tool’s flex so the policy can map force error to angle correction.
Robotic Hand Tool Use with Contact-Based.how:
The problem: Trajectories vary wildly across cucumbers and demoing humans; blindly copying joint angles fails. But the contact force and approach angle are stable and task-relevant.

The mechanism:

  1. Human demonstrates peeling a vegetable while wearing an optical tactile sensor (GelSight) on the tool tip; record RGB contact images, 3D contact geometry, and normal force at 30 Hz.
  2. Extract the contact profile: approach angle (θ = 35°), peak contact force (F = 1.2 N ± 0.3 N), stroke length, and peel-lift timing.
  3. Calibration phase: the robot makes 3 calibration pokes on a test vegetable; measure the tool-tip deflection vs. force, fit a spring model (K = 1400 N/m).
  4. Execution: run admittance control: if actual force is 0.1 N too high, adjust the tool angle by –0.5°, computed via the stiffness model.
  5. Use the force-torque wrist feedback in a PID loop to maintain target force within ±0.2 N.

Why it works: The tool is an intermediary; controlling through it requires understanding its stiffness and mapping force errors to position corrections. Admittance control lets the robot ‘feel’ the vegetable and adjust on the fly without trajectory re-planning.

Hierarchical RL for Articulated Tool Man.narr: Operating a multi-joint tool — scissors, pliers, a pump — requires more than grasping; the robot must coordinate fingers to actuate the tool’s mechanism. A hierarchical policy learns a low-level primitive (e.g., ‘squeeze the scissors closed’) and a high-level strategy that decides which primitive to apply when. The tool-affordance encoder learns to recognize the tool from images and conditions the high-level policy, so one agent can handle scissors, pliers, and pumps.
Hierarchical RL for Articulated Tool Man.how:
The problem: A monolithic policy must learn the joint coordination for every tool variant; the space is huge. Decomposing into reusable primitives reduces it.

The mechanism:

  1. Define low-level primitives: ‘grasp the handle’, ‘squeeze’, ‘open’, ‘rotate wrist’. Each is a short, fixed-duration RL policy trained separately on multiple tool instances.
  2. A tool-affordance encoder (CNN + MLP) maps RGB image to a latent tool embedding (32-D vector).
  3. Train a high-level policy that takes (latent tool embedding, task goal, hand state) and outputs which primitive to execute next and for how long.
  4. High-level runs at 1 Hz; primitives run at 20 Hz. The high-level policy learns the sequence for the task (cut, rotate, cut again).
  5. Expose the tool embedding to both training environments, so the policy adapts to tool variants unseen at training time.

Why it works: Hierarchical decomposition scales to multiple tools; the affordance encoder generalizes across similar tools (e.g., different scissors brands), and primitives are reusable. The policy learns *strategy*, not low-level finger choreography.

Implicit Physics-aware Policy for Dynami.narr: Rope, hoses, and soft-body tools behave nothing like rigid graspers: their state is distributed (not a point), and their dynamics are hard to model from first principles. A robot manipulating with a rope must feel the rope’s state through forces at its end and adapt. Implicit system identification learns the tool’s effective stiffness and damping online, then a policy uses that learned model to decide how hard to pull and where.
Implicit Physics-aware Policy for Dynami.how:
The problem: Soft-body tools have infinite degrees of freedom; trying to model them explicitly is intractable. But the robot can probe the tool and learn its local dynamics.

The mechanism:

  1. The robot holds one end of a rope; at each step, it applies a small test displacement (2 cm step) and records the reaction force (F_t) and rope extension (dx_t).
  2. Fit a local spring-damper model: F = K_eff * dx + D_eff * d(dx)/dt, solving for K_eff and D_eff via least-squares on a sliding window of recent measurements.
  3. Use the learned K_eff and D_eff to predict the effect of a candidate pull direction and magnitude; score candidates by how well they move the rope end toward the goal.
  4. Execute the best action; re-identify the model on the next timestep. This is online system ID in the loop.

Why it works: Implicit identification sidesteps the need for a global model; the robot learns just enough local dynamics to make good decisions. Continuous re-identification adapts to rope state changes (tangles, stretching, etc.) without explicit modeling.

MOKA: Open-World Manipulation through Ma.narr: A screwdriver affords unscrewing; a spoon affords scooping. The robot must infer the affordance from the instruction and the tool image, then grasp accordingly. VLMs are powerful but not grounded in the robot’s embodiment. MOKA turns affordance reasoning into a visual question: show the VLM the image and ask ‘where should I grab this tool to [verb]?’; the VLM marks the region.
MOKA: Open-World Manipulation through Ma.how:
The problem: Open-vocabulary grasping requires reasoning from language to tool geometry to grasp points; a single vision network can’t do this without massive retraining on every new task-tool pair.

The mechanism:

  1. Parse the instruction into a task verb: ‘turn the screw’ → ‘screw’; ‘eat the soup’ → ‘scoop’.
  2. Capture an RGB image of the tool in the hand.
  3. Prompt a VLM (e.g., GPT-4V, LLaVA) with: ‘To [verb] effectively, where on this [tool name] should the gripper hold? Mark the region.’
  4. The VLM returns spatial coordinates or a bounding box on the image (sometimes via auxiliary vision models like SAM for segmentation).
  5. Backproject the marked region to 3D using depth; sample grasps within that region; filter and execute the best.

Why it works: VLMs have broad world knowledge of tool use; querying them avoids per-tool training. Visual prompting grounds the abstract reasoning in the actual tool image, avoiding hallucinations. Spatial grounding via depth makes the reasoning actionable.

ORLA*: Mobile-Manipulator Rearrangement.narr: Rearranging 12 objects in a bin to specific goal poses is an NP-hard scheduling problem: picking the wrong object first can block the goal pose of a later one, forcing backtracking. Naive nearest-neighbor ordering wastes 3 extra picks. ORLA* is lazy A* with a learned heuristic: expand only the most promising nodes in the rearrangement graph, guided by an MLP trained on random scenes to predict how many picks remain.
ORLA*: Mobile-Manipulator Rearrangement.how:
The problem: Graph search over rearrangement orderings is huge; A* needs a good heuristic to prune the space.

The mechanism:

  1. Build a directed dependency graph: compute which objects block which goal poses (ray-cast from each target, count intersecting objects).
  2. A rearrangement sequence is any ordering that respects dependencies (don’t pick a blocker after its target).
  3. State space: current scene (which objects have been moved). Edges: pick the next object, move it to goal, update scene.
  4. Train an MLP heuristic on 50,000 random scenes: predict the minimum picks needed to finish rearrangement.
  5. Run A* with lazy expansion: sort open nodes by f = g + h(state), expand only the best node, defer expanding children until needed.
  6. Lazy expansion avoids expanding the full branching tree; only the most promising paths are explored.

Why it works: Lazy evaluation and learned heuristics together prune the search space to tractable size. The learned heuristic captures the structure of rearrangement (how many blockers typically remain) without hand-tuning costs. Dependency analysis gives a tight lower bound on picks.

Match Policy: From Point-Cloud Registrat.narr: Re-planning each pick is slow. An alternative: cast action inference as a registration problem. Given a goal configuration (a stored image of the target scene), warp the current point cloud to match it and extract the motion as a rigid transformation. A small neural network learns to correct for non-rigid deformation and occlusion, making the approach fast (80 ms per pick) and generalizable. The key insight is that point-cloud alignment implicitly solves both ‘what to pick’ and ‘where to place it’.
Match Policy: From Point-Cloud Registrat.how:
The problem: Re-planning is slow; hard-coding pick sequences is brittle. Point-cloud registration is fast and geometric, but only works for rigid objects.

The mechanism:

  1. Collect demonstrations: for each task, record RGB-D and store a target scene image.
  2. Align the current point cloud to the target using iterative closest point (ICP), initialized with a coarse CNN match.
  3. Extract the rigid transformation (rotation + translation) from the best alignment.
  4. Train a small MLP to refine the transformation: input is the current cloud, target, and ICP residuals; output is a correction delta.
  5. The MLP learns to account for non-rigidities (cloth, deformation) and occlusions (some targets are unreachable from the current view).
  6. Convert the transformation to gripper motion: use the rotation to infer grasp orientation, the translation to infer target pose.

Why it works: Registration-as-policy is fast (no replanning) and generalizes across object instances (it’s based on geometry, not appearance). The learned MLP adds just enough flexibility for non-rigidity without derailing the method. Storing demos as target scenes is simpler than storing trajectories.

Towards Generalizable Vision-Language Ma.narr: A policy trained on mug-picking in one location fails on mug-placing in another. Real generalization requires understanding the scene context: where objects are, what obstacles exist, which surfaces are stable. 3D-LOTUS is a 3D vision-language policy that attends to the full point cloud and natural-language instructions, learning task-relevant features that transfer across new objects and goal regions without retraining.
Towards Generalizable Vision-Language Ma.how:
The problem: Vision-language policies trained on task sequences don’t generalize to new scenes because they overfit to object appearance and absolute positions.

The mechanism:

  1. Encode the instruction in a language model (e.g., CLIP); extract a task embedding (128-D).
  2. Encode the scene as a point cloud; use a 3D transformer to compute per-point attention weights, conditioning on the task embedding and current gripper pose.
  3. Aggregate point features weighted by attention; concatenate with task embedding and gripper state to form the policy input.
  4. The policy outputs 7-D actions: 3D gripper velocity + gripper open/close + 3D rotation velocity.
  5. Train on 10k demonstrations of (scene, instruction, action) tuples across multiple objects and poses.
  6. At test time, the learned attention mechanism generalizes: points that are relevant to the task (e.g., ‘clear the center’ → focus on central obstruction) are up-weighted, regardless of object identity.

Why it works: Attention-based 3D reasoning is invariant to object appearance and absolute position; it learns what parts of the scene matter for the task. Language conditioning grounds the attention, avoiding hallucinations. Training on diverse scenes teaches the policy scene-dependent reasoning.

Hook-Based Aerial Payload Grasping from.narr: An aerial vehicle (drone or helicopter) cannot hover indefinitely; it must grab a payload mid-flight. The payload is on the ground or on a moving platform, and the aerial vehicle is moving. The grasp window is milliseconds. Trajectory optimization pre-computes a collision-free path and the optimal timing for the hook to latch, given the platform motion and aerial dynamics.
Hook-Based Aerial Payload Grasping from.how:
The problem: Aerial grasping is a constrained trajectory problem: the aerial vehicle must approach at a reachable speed, the hook must latch at the right angle, and the payload must not collide with the platform or the vehicle.

The mechanism:

  1. Model the aerial vehicle as a rigid body with mass m and rotor thrust limits (max acceleration a_max).
  2. Model the hook as a rigid link attached to the vehicle; define the grasp point and approach direction.
  3. Predict the platform motion: it may be stationary, moving at constant velocity, or following a known trajectory.
  4. Formulate trajectory optimization: find the aerial path and latch time that minimize time to grasp and energy, subject to: collision-free (vehicle + hook avoid platform), feasibility (acceleration within rotor limits), and grasping success (hook latches at the right angle).
  5. Solve using iterative LQR or DDP; warm-start with a heuristic (approach from above, descend at max acceleration).

Why it works: Trajectory optimization couples the vehicle dynamics and grasp geometry, finding a solution that is dynamically feasible and collision-aware. Pre-computing the trajectory offline allows real-time execution; replanning only if the platform motion changes drastically.

AffordGrasp: In-Context Affordance Reaso.narr: A knife affords cutting (grasp the handle) and handover (grasp the blade). A force-closure-optimal grip ignores the task. The robot must reason from the instruction (‘hand it to someone’) backward to the object part (‘blade’), then to the grasp points. AffordGrasp queries a VLM in-context to reason about affordances, then grounds the reasoning with part segmentation and grasp sampling.
AffordGrasp: In-Context Affordance Reaso.how:
The problem: Task-oriented grasping requires chaining language → semantics → geometry → physics; no single model does all four without massive retraining per task.

The mechanism:

  1. Instruction: ‘hand the scissors to the person’.
  2. Query VLM (e.g., GPT-4V) in-context: show image + ask ‘Which part of the scissors should I grip to hand safely?’; it responds with the part and reasoning.
  3. Ground the part: use open-vocabulary segmentation (OWL-ViT or SAM) to find the pixel region corresponding to the VLM’s answer (e.g., ‘blade, away from the cutting edge’).
  4. Grasp generation: sample 256 grasps using GraspNet (or similar); filter to keep only grasps whose contact points fall within the grounded region mask (90% overlap threshold).
  5. Quality ranking: keep the 18 highest-quality grasps (force-closure, stability); execute the best.

Why it works: VLM reasoning is broad and task-aware; grounding it with segmentation makes it actionable; filtering by geometric constraints ensures the grasp is actually on the intended part. Multi-stage composition is more interpretable and reliable than end-to-end learning.

RT-Affordance: Affordances as Intermedia.narr: Learning the full visuomotor policy from language and images is hard; representations matter. Intermediate representations like affordance keypoints (e.g., ‘handle location for cutting’) bridge language and action. RT-Affordance predicts affordance keypoints as an intermediate layer, enabling efficient learning from web-scale data and transfer to new objects unseen at training time.
RT-Affordance: Affordances as Intermedia.how:
The problem: End-to-end policies are sample-inefficient and don’t generalize; intermediate representations help but are hard to define for every task.

The mechanism:

  1. Pre-train an affordance detector on web images: given a task description (e.g., ‘cutting’), predict keypoints like ‘blade handle’, ‘blade edge’, ‘direction of motion’.
  2. Fine-tune the detector on a small number of robot demos (100-1000 trajectories).
  3. Train a manipulation policy that takes (task description, current observation, predicted keypoints) and outputs actions.
  4. At test time, the policy sees new objects: the pre-trained affordance detector generalizes (it’s seen scissors before, even if not this brand), guiding the policy.
  5. Evaluate on object variations: different sizes, materials, orientations.

Why it works: Affordances are task-specific but object-agnostic; learning them from web data transfers to new objects. Intermediate representations decouple perception and control, allowing each to be trained with different data. The policy can ignore object-specific details and focus on task execution.

AffordGen: Diverse Demonstrations via Af.narr: A single human demo of grasping a coffee mug is not enough to train a generalizable policy; the robot needs to see handles at different angles. Collecting 100 demos of every object is infeasible. AffordGen uses dense correspondences (DINOv2 features) to find similar affordances across object instances, then transfers grasps from the demo objects to new objects by aligning their affordances, synthetically generating diverse demonstrations.
AffordGen: Diverse Demonstrations via Af.how:
The problem: Data augmentation for grasping is hard; you can’t simply rotate a grasp trajectory—the geometry changes. But affordances (handle, body) are consistent across instances.

The mechanism:

  1. Collect 10 human demos of grasping diverse objects (mugs, bottles, cans, etc.).
  2. Extract dense per-pixel correspondence using DINOv2 features; group pixels into semantic affordance regions (handle vs. body).
  3. At test time, given a new object, compute its DINOv2 features and match to the closest demo object.
  4. Identify corresponding affordance regions (demo ‘handle’ matches to test ‘handle’).
  5. Warp the demo grasp trajectory by aligning the corresponding affordance regions: compute a thin-plate-spline deformation that maps demo handle to test handle.
  6. Execute the warped grasp.

Why it works: Self-supervised correspondences (DINOv2) generalize across object categories because they capture semantic structure, not appearance. Warping trajectories via affordance alignment is more reliable than geometry-based warping (which can fail on different shapes); it works because grasping is about affordance, not object geometry.

SemSegGrasp: Task-Oriented Grasping via.narr: Affordance reasoning can be simplified: first, semantically segment the object (which parts matter?), then grasp the right part. Decoupling segmentation from grasp detection lets each model be trained on its own data. SemSegGrasp segments semantic parts in images, then samples grasps only on the task-relevant part, unifying affordance and physics constraints.
SemSegGrasp: Task-Oriented Grasping via.how:
The problem: End-to-end task-aware grasping requires understanding both semantics and physics; jointly training is inefficient and data-hungry.

The mechanism:

  1. Train a semantic segmentation network on labeled object-part datasets (e.g., PartNet, with labels like ‘handle’, ‘blade’, ‘body’).
  2. Given a task (e.g., ‘cut’), map it to the relevant part (via a fixed rule or a small learned classifier): ‘cut’ → ‘handle’.
